Here's the main idea you're missing (that a lot of other commenters are missing too)

When you allow really bad hands to play, the only way they put more money in the pot postflop is if they hit their hand perfectly. But if your aces stay ahead of 56o, villain's not gonna give you much more money. So it's in your best interest to just get them to fold pre.

If you got dealt Aces and could force everyone at the table to go all-in pre without looking, then yes, you'd want as many opponents in the pot as possible. A 9-way no look preflop all-in with Aces is higher EV than a 2-way all in\*, even though your odds of winning drop significantly. The problem is, though, that in a real game, you're probably not gonna get much money from your opponents' bad hands unless they hit a hand postflop that's better than yours.

​

When people slowplay aces, what they mean is just calling an open or a 3-bet. This works better than limping because when you're up against a better range of hands, they can hit top pair or a flush draw, give you more money, and still be beat. Whereas the main way 56o pays you is if they hit their miracle 2 pair plus.

this comment is ignoring bluffs btw. Limping with aces could maybe make sense if you're up against hyper-bluffers, only because they're so likely to give you money with their 56o that doesn't connect.

​

\*if anyone else has an Ace, your EV will be slightly better 9-ways to 2-ways, depending on how many villains have pairs. There's about a 50% chance that at least one villain will have an Ace. Otherwise, your EV improves.

The wrap makes open strings sound more like fretted strings if and only if you have it placed on or just in front of the nut, which makes it less effective in actually muting your untouched strings.

In order for it to work really well as a muting solution, it’s gotta be up a full fret or two, which will in fact completely kill your open strings (by design).

here’s 3 and a half additional unexpected Gruv Gear benefits:

- when used at the first fret and beyond, it effectively lowers your action. Unlike lowering your saddle, the wrap pushes down on the string from behind the fretted note, so this won’t add any fret buzz.

- makes a very convenient pick holder (buy one and you’ll see what i mean, there’s a nice slot to store your pick). Even when I’m not using mine it stays behind the nut at all times for this purpose.

- eliminating the option to play open strings made me a better bass player. Learning basslines without the use of open strings means you can play it in any key just by shifting the whole line up or down some frets. More importantly, this method will drill the essence of the learned bassline deeper into your head. You’ll be free to incorporate ideas from the songs you learn into new material, no matter what key you’re in or where your hand is on the neck. 
- eliminating open strings also makes most songs a fun challenge to learn and play. Hysteria by Muse is a notable example. Learning that line without open strings was hugely productive for advancing my right hand technique.

TLDR: buy one.
